questions.problem:
Consider the function $y=(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}.$ Its derivative is given by 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}\cdot g(x).
$$

Find the function $g(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x))+(x)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $g(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x\operatorname{tan}⁡x.$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $y=(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.$ Its derivative is given by 

$$
{y}^{′}=-(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x-1}\cdot g(x).
$$

Find the function $g(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\,(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x))+(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\cdot (-\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\operatorname{csc}⁡x)) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{cot}⁡x \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{cot}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =-(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\,(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =-(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x-1}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x.$

questions.worked_solution:
We have the function 

$$
y=(2x+3)^{x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((2x+3)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3))+(x)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3)+x\cdot (\frac{1}{2x+3}\cdot 2) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3)+\frac{2x}{2x+3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3)+\frac{2x}{2x+3})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(2x+3)^{x}:$    

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(2x+3)^{x}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3)+\frac{2x}{2x+3}) \\  & =(2x+3)^{x}\cdot (\frac{(2x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3)}{2x+3}+\frac{2x}{2x+3}) \\  & =(2x+3)^{x-1}\cdot ((2x+3)\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3)+2x).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=0$ equals the function's derivative at the corresponding point.

We have the function 

$$
y={(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =({x}^{2}+1)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\,(({x}^{2}+1)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})) \\ \frac{1}{y}\,{y}^{′} & =({x}^{2}+1)^{′}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})+({x}^{2}+1)\,{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1}))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\,{y}^{′} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})+({x}^{2}+1)\,(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x+1}}\cdot \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2x+1}}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y\,(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2x+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y={(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2x+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y={(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}$ at $x=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m={y}^{′}{|}_{x=0} & ={(\sqrt{2(0)+1})}^{(0)^{2}+1}(0\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2(0)+1)+\frac{(0)^{2}+1}{2(0)+1}) \\  & =1\cdot (0\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-y(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))+\operatorname{csc}⁡(x))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))+\operatorname{csc}⁡(x))\end{aligned}
